newsitem.title: USA: Opponents call for U.S. ban on Internet gambling.
newsitem.headline: Opponents call for U.S. ban on Internet gambling.

text.p: Opponents of Internet gambling told a Senate panel on Monday that online wagering should be banned because it defies regulation, endangers consumers and interferes with states' rights.
Sen. Richard Bryan, a Nevada Democrat, told a Senate Judiciary subcommittee that Internet gambling violates states' rights to choose what activities to permit within their borders.

"Some states have chosen to permit gaming and others have chosen to prohibit it. That should be their choice," Bryan said. "By its very nature, however, the Internet cannot be constrained by state or national boundaries."

Wisconsin Attorney General James Doyle said he welcomed the anti-gambling legislation and called for the negotiation of international agreements to protect U.S. residents from offshore Internet casinos.

"Because (Internet gambling) is unregulated, consumers don't know who is on the other end of the connection," Doyle said. "The odds can be easily manipulated and there is no guarantee that fair payouts will occur."

The opponents of Internet gambling were speaking at a hearing to consider a bill introduced by subcommittee chairman Jon Kyl, Republican of Arizona, that would ban Internet gaming and introduce criminal penalties.
The bill would allow local, state and federal officials to "pull the plug" on the telephone service and Internet presence of computer gambling businesses, Doyle said.
Other proponents lauded the legislation for keeping minors clear of gambling and generally limiting the spread of wagering.
The bill, introduced by Kyl in March, would extend penalties to companies that provide online gambling. It asserts federal jurisdiction over Internet wagering as a form of interstate commerce.
"This bill is essentially a straightforward application of existing law to a new venue," Kyl said.
Lawmakers have continously extended gambling restrictions to cover evolving communications technology, Kyl said.
"Extending the prohibition to gambling on the Internet is no different than extending it to the telephone or 'wire,' as happened when those innovations came along," he said.
Only supporters of the bill had been invited to testify, but some opponents of the legislation attended the proceedings.
"For people to say there is no way to regulate this is just not right," Sue Schneider, chairwoman of the Interactive Gaming Council, an industry association, told Reuters.
Most online casinos are licensed by the country or territory in which they are located, Schneider said. In addition, she said, most are bonded to guarantee payouts.
